answer: Use the read-only spectrum-monitoring command: show spectrum-monitoring-<name>/<direction>/<center-frequency> [width] [lower-frequency] [upper-frequency] [target-actual-power] [power-actual] [psd-actual], for example show spectrum-monitoring-1-7-dwdm-line2/egress/191968750. It is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is a string 0..64; direction is ingress or egress, default egress, and only egress is currently supported; center-frequency is the band slice center frequency in MHz and is managed by the system. width is the received NMC width in MHz, default 50000. lower-frequency and upper-frequency give the Media Channel edges in MHz. power-actual is the currently received power in dBm, default -99; -99dBm means the power has not yet been measured by the OCM at the DGE2 card, or no power was detected (or there is no appropriate fiber-connection). For egress, power-actual is calibrated at the DWDM Line port output, the same reference point where target power is defined. target-actual-power is the power calculated by ATPS, default -99dBm, and is only relevant when target-power-setting = auto. psd-actual is the calculated Power Spectral Density in nW/GHz with 2 digit precision, default not-applicable, and does not depend on the spectral width.

Read the contention-check-status attribute of the super-channel. It is settable on add (add super-channel-<name> carriers <value> carrier-mode <value> [label] [admin-state] [alarm-report-control] [contention-check-status]) and readable with show super-channel-<name> contention-check-status. The Contention Check state is set via DNA in openwave mode and takes the values pending, success, overridden and failk, with default pending. It is only applicable if openwave-contention-check is enabled at the super-channel-group level; openwave-contention-check enables the DNA assisted contention control mechanism in openwave mode, takes true or false and defaults to false. So enable openwave-contention-check on the super-channel-group first (add -m super-channel-group-<name> ... openwave-contention-check <value>), otherwise the status stays meaningless. The related line-system-mode indicates the L1 to L0 power control mode and is openwave. Both commands run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

-m is the merge flag: 'Merge configuration (the command will not fail if the entity already exists)'. The add command for super-channel-group works in merge mode only, so the -m flag is required. A merge is a best effort add: if the target entity does not exist it is created, and if it already exists it is updated with whatever attributes are present on the add command. The full form is add -m super-channel-group-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <lock|unlock|maintenance>] [auto-in-service-enabled <value>] [valid-signal-time <value>] [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>] [line-system-mode <value>] [openwave-contention-check <value>]. Defaults are admin-state unlock, alarm-report-control allowed, auto-in-service-enabled false, line-system-mode openwave and valid-signal-time 480 minutes (range 1..7200). The same -m merge flag applies to comm-channel.

Use show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [status] [supported-subtypes], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. carrier-mode is an acronymized code (handle) indicating the optical carrier line mode 4-tuple, string length 1..15, formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>, for example 600E.84P, 100X.73U or 325M.66P. capacity is the net capacity of the optical carrier in gbps, so that column answers the capacity question. client-mode gives the digital client modes mapped into and transported by the carriers within the superchannel and is ethernet or ethernet-otn. baud-rate is the modulated symbol rate. application is the optical transport application ID the mode is optimized for, string 1..15. compatibility-id identifies carrier modes that can be applied simultaneously, and status is the state of the carrier mode. supported-subtypes lists the subtypes each carrier mode supports, string 0..32, maximum 20 elements.

Use show supported-gain-range-<name>/<gain-range-type> [gain-range-min] [gain-range-max], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. gain-range-type is the type of gain-range and takes low, high or standard. gain-range-min is the minimum settable gain-target for that type of range ('standard'/'low'/'high') and gain-range-max is the maximum settable gain-target for that range; both are of type gain-value with no stated default. The name key is documented as a flag to enable or disable access control with values true or false and default false. So to see the actual dB limits behind low, standard and high, query the entity for the gain-range-type of interest and read gain-range-min and gain-range-max.

Different power profiles are supported to reflect different scenarios when using a card. The user is able to define, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. To see what a card type offers, use show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. card-type is the card type (string) and name is the profile name (string). profile-description is a description of the profile, string length 0..255. power-draw is the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power, of type decimal64. default is true or false and tells you whether that profile is the default one. No defaults are stated for these read-only attributes.

The router ID comes from router-id-mode, which is a flag indicating whether the router-id is the loopback IP. It takes use-loopback or manual and defaults to use-loopback, so by default the instance takes the loopback IP. If you set router-id-mode manual you supply the value explicitly with router-id, which accepts an IPv4 or IPv6 address; 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6. The syntax is add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], and both attributes can be changed later with set bgp-instance-<instance-id>. instance-id is a string of length 1..255, local-as is mandatory on add and is a number in the range 1..4294967295, and description is a string 0..128. Example: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The bgp-neighbor defaults are connect-retry-interval 120 seconds (range 1..65535, the interval between attempts to establish a session), hold-time 90 seconds (range 3..65535, typically set to 3x the keepalive-interval) and keepalive-interval 30 seconds (range 1..21845, typically 1/3 of the hold-time). negotiated-hold-time is read-only, range 0..65535, default 0. Yes, you can authenticate the session: secure-session sets the authentication method to none or TCP-MD5, defaulting to none, and password carries the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII format, string 0..80. Syntax: add bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address> peer-as <value> [afi-safis <value>] [enabled <value>] [description <value>] [secure-session <value>] [password <value>] [connect-retry-interval <value>] [hold-time <value>] [keepalive-interval <value>]. peer-as is 1..4294967295 and enabled defaults to true. session-state shows Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established or Close, default Idle.

The routes to be advertised to an external AS must already exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. If the prefix is not present in the IGP tables, you must configure a blackhole static route for it: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole, for example add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> special-next-hop blackhole (special-next-hop takes the value blackhole and is available on ipv4-static-route and ipv6-static-route in add, set and show). The bgp-network object itself is created with add bgp-network-<instance-id>/<remote-address>/<network-prefix>, where instance-id is a string 1..255, remote-address is the BGP peer address in IPv4 or IPv6 format (0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported) and network-prefix is a decimal number 1..64, or 128. A maximum of 100 bgp-network MOs can be configured.

The comm-channel mtu is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, an unsigned 16-bit integer. The range is platform dependent: 1280..1500 octets on the 1830 GX G30 only, and 1280..9202 octets on the 1830 GX G40 only. The default is 1500, except that on 1830 GX G40 the default is 1518 for these interface types: DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4. Pre-condition: mtu is available only when mode is L3 (mode takes L1 for L1 ETH User Channel Mode, L2 for the L2 iGCC interface, or L3 for L3 IP Mode, default L3). Set it with add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [... mtu <value> ...] or set comm-channel-<name> mtu <value>. Related L3-only attributes are mru (64..1500 octets, default 1500), restart-timer (1..10 seconds, default 3), max-failure (2..10, default 5) and peer-address (default 0.0.0.0).

LLDP is not on by default. lldp-admin-status defaults to disabled, meaning the LLDP agent neither transmits nor receives LLDP frames on the port; the other values are tx-only (transmits but does not store remote system information), rx-only (receives but does not transmit) and tx-and-rx. It cannot be modified if mode is L1. Enable it with, for example, set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. lldp-transmit-interval is the LLDP Tx TLV interval, 1..16383 seconds, default 30. lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects which interface IP is advertised as the management address (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only), L0-MGMT); it is empty by default and applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx. For speed, auto-negotiation defaults to enabled. duplex-mode (default full), rate (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum) and flow-control (default disabled) are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled; read back operational-rate, operational-duplex-mode and operational-flow-control. mtu is 1280..1500 octets, default 1500.

Use the global dhcp-relay command: set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>] and show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, with default disabled. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses as an IPv4 or IPv6 server address; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, or both at once with set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3. This is the global setting; per-interface enabling is done separately with set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true, which obeys the global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns command has assignment-method, which indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. It takes manual, dhcp or both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts name servers from DHCP as well as manually configured ones. Configure it with set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and read it back with show dns. enabled is the flag indicating if DNS is enabled, true or false, default true. search is the DNS-search-suffix name, a string of length 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot; to clear it, set the string to an empty string. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Individual servers carry their own origin (dhcp or manual) on the dns-server object.

Add a name server with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server. The origin attribute records the DNS address assignment method: dhcp indicates a DNS address that has been assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address has been manually configured. The default is manual. So show dns-server-<address> [origin], or show dns-server for the list, tells you which entries came from DHCP. You can also convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute with set dns-server-<address> origin manual. Remove a server with delete dns-server-<address>. Example: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the if-dhcp-relay object: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true, and check it with show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface, takes true or false, and defaults to false. It obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (its default is disabled) and a server-address configured for relaying to work. Example: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true. The command runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. The same per-interface control appears on the interface object as if-dhcp-relay, false or true, default false.

By default a new interface is static and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> [...], ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive IPv4 and IPv6 packets. protection-mode is the user given protection mode and takes unknown (transient, output only), protected (protected by redundant ports) or unprotected (no port redundancy); its default is protected. The separate read-only protection-state reports the current protection of the interface and defaults to unknown. Other defaults: proxy-arp-enabled false (only applicable to the DCN interface), if-dhcp-relay false, admin-state unlock, oper-state disabled, alarm-report-control allowed. if-name is a string 0..64 and if-type is ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp or hdlc. Example: set interface-DCN protection-mode protected.

Yes, that is what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings a destination and the result takes action on configured static-routes. Create one with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action to take when monitoring goes into the 'failed' state, takes none or withdraw, and defaults to withdraw, so the route is pulled by default. static-route is the list of connected static routes for this instance, a string with a maximum of 10 elements. destination is the remote host to monitor (ipv4-address or ipv6-address). next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address, and the monitoring instance is not active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is the time between two consecutive pings, 0..60 seconds, default 5. drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1. enabled is true or false, default true. The route side shows monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>; netmask is mandatory and is the subnet specified as a netmask for that address, and only valid netmasks are allowed. Example: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0', or on the DCN port add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0. Read it with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and remove it with delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. These addresses are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback addresses), and addresses beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). origin is read-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. if-name is a string 0..64; use '?' after ipv4-address- to list the available interfaces. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. Set it on add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. A discard route is created with special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (default blackhole), usable in add, set and show. Blackhole static routes are needed because routes advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, but not by BGP itself; for prefixes not present in IGP tables you configure a blackhole static route. Other attributes: advertised true or false, default false (when true the route is advertised in the routing protocol, and for OSPF it is advertised as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR); origin manual or dhcp, default manual; interface must be bound to the same vrf given on the static route. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165.

Almost, but the mandatory argument is prefix-length rather than netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin], delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported only on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. origin is read-only and reports static (statically configured, for example via NETCONF or the CLI), dhcp (assigned by a DHCP server) or auto-config (created by autoconfiguration), with default static. if-name is a string 0..64; use '?' after ipv6-address- to see the available interfaces. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>] and name DCN-B on the interface parameter, for example add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B (the DCN equivalent is add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN). The VRF bound to the interface must match the vrf given on the static route. distance is 1..255, default 1; advertised is true or false, default false; origin is manual or dhcp, default manual; special-next-hop takes blackhole for discard routes. monitoring-state reports unmonitored, ok or failed. Access is Operational and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]. This retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component; there may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each management address must have a distinct 'management address type' (subtype) and 'management address' (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor (an instance) and direction is ingress or egress. address-subtype is the type of management address identifier encoding used in the associated address attribute (string), and address is the string used to identify the management address component associated with the remote system, length 0..64, whose purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype describes the basis of the interface associated with the address and is unknown, if-index or system-port-number; if-id is the integer interface number; address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity advertised by the remote system agent, string 0..128. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

They carry the same attribute set but differ in key structure and in which side's LLDP ports they report. management-address is keyed show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>, including a direction key of ingress or egress. management-address-local drops the direction key: show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>, and its example, show management-address-local, is described as viewing the management address information from the local LLDP ports. Both take the same read-only attributes: if-subtype (unknown, meaning the interface is not known; if-index, an identifier based on the ifIndex MIB object; or system-port-number, based on the system port numbering convention), if-id (the integer interface number) and address-oid (the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity advertised by the remote system agent, string 0..128; for management-address-local that field is currently an empty string). Both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, that is the use-as-source attribute of the networking command. It names the interface to use as the source address and is a string of length 0..64, used in both set and show, with no stated default. Configure it with set networking [use-as-source <value>], for example set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and read it back with show networking [use-as-source] or simply show networking. The command is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and use-as-source is the only parameter the networking object takes.

show networking-services. This command shows the list of network services and takes no parameters at all. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and show is its only verb, so there is no set or delete form and no per-instance key to supply. Example: show networking-services. For related network-wide settings use the separate networking command, which carries use-as-source, the interface to use as the source address.
